passages.title: Loss and the return to Bethlehem
passages.summary: Famine takes Elimelech’s household to Moab. After three deaths, Naomi returns. Ruth stays with her, while Orpah returns home. Grief and chosen loyalty shape the opening. Orpah receives Naomi’s blessing. Her departure does not make her an enemy.
passages.uncertainty: The map shows the named town and broad region. It does not identify private buildings or an ancient road.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies faith through loss. Its application does not promise that every bereaved person will remarry.

passages.title: Ruth gleans in Boaz’s field
passages.summary: Ruth gathers leftover grain. Boaz provides protection, food, and additional grain. Naomi recognizes his connection with their family. Gleaning means collecting grain left after harvest. The account makes safety, work, and practical care central to household survival.
passages.uncertainty: The map shows the named town and broad region. It does not identify private buildings or an ancient road.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies kindness and trust. Consider how practical help changes the conditions another person faces.

passages.title: The request at the threshing floor
passages.summary: Naomi proposes a plan. Ruth approaches Boaz at night and asks for his protection. He promises action after consulting a nearer relative. Ruth speaks directly about family redemption. Readers debate the scene’s implications. The text does not explicitly describe a sexual act.
passages.uncertainty: The map shows the named town and broad region. It does not identify private buildings or an ancient road.

lds.text: The older manual reads Ruth’s request as a marriage proposal. Keep that interpretation distinct from unstated details.

passages.title: The gate agreement and Obed’s birth
passages.summary: Boaz consults the nearer relative and witnesses at the gate. He marries Ruth. Obed is born, and the closing genealogy reaches David. Public witnesses connect household care with recognized responsibility. The genealogy is the book’s claim about ancestry, not an independently verified record.
passages.uncertainty: The map shows the named town and broad region. It does not identify private buildings or an ancient road.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares Ruth and Boaz with Jesus Christ. This Christian reading is separate from the ancient narrated transaction.
